serve bid, and unless the offers reach that, the property is not sold. That is a business way of disposing of a piece of property, and the Minister of the Interior should have proceeded in that way. He has not told ns that he got any information whatever except what he got from the surveyor, and I am informed that if all the facts were known his report would not carry very much weight. The Minister of the Interior and also the Minister of Public Works might learn a good lesson if he would study the methods adopted by the government of Ontario in disposing of public property. Let me give one illustration, and I could multiply it by scores. They had a piece of property a short time ago for sale. The highest offer was $50,000. But the Prime Minister said: I have private information that this property is worth a great deal more. And although they were his political friends who had offered the $50,000, he said: I am trustee for the whole of the people of Ontario, I am informed this property is worth a great deal more than $50,000 and you cannot have it. What was the result? He re-advertised the property for sale, and the very same men came forward and offered him $178,000 for the property. Then take public contracts. A short time ago, the Ontario government advertised for the construction of a public building. The lowest tender was for a certain sum, but the Minister of Public Works said, I have had that matter investigated, I am informed that building can be erected for much less, we will build it ourselves. They engaged a foreman and put up the building and it cost onv 60 per cent of the lowest tender. That is only one or two instances to show that in. Ontario public affairs are carried on in a businesslike manner.
This illustration you have just had of the sale of lands in Manitoba-and we had a dozen such cases last year-shows us that this government does not dispose of public properties in a businesslike manner. I do not wish to go into the particulars of the tenders but I submit that the minister has not-so far as we can judge from what information he has condescended to give us on this matter-taken a businesslike manner to dispose of this property in the interests of the poor Indians.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I suppose it is the privilege of an hon. member to say in this House anything he pleases. But since mv hon. friend has been so very critical in this matter, let me repeat that in this particular case, the land was advertised in the public newspapers and was sold by public auction in parcels of 160 acres each, or 60 to 70 different parcels. It was valued, when surveyed, by a competent man and sold at a prft-e above his valuation, and the transaction was in all respects quite on a par with the best illustration the hon. gentle-

man has given the House. Let me point out that the only difference., judging by the instances he gave us, is this, that there must be a difficult lot of people which the Ontario government have to deal with in Ontario.

Will the hon. minister, when the main estimates come up, bring down a list of the papers in which these lands were advertised, also a list of the purchasers and the prices paid? Some of my hon. friends behind me asked if they were advertised in the Selkirk papers and the hon. gentleman could not answer the question.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have no objection whatever.
How much was paid the auctioneer and who was he?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He wras paid one half per cent of the selling price, not to exceed in all $200. I cannot give his name just now.
Does the minister undertake to say that he considers $6 per acre a fair price for this land?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, I think that any land advertised in the public press for a reasonable time and offered for sale within a'distance of 25 miles of Winnipeg is absolutely certain to bring its full value at that particular time.

I am somewhat surprised at the minister's statement regarding the advertisement of those lands. As I said a few' moments ago, although these lands had been advertised, there were conditions surrounding the whole transactions which practically frightened away ordinary purchasers. There was a letter'from the department which seems to have been entirely overlooked by the minister. That letter was practically a warning to the people that the Indians had nothing to sell, and the average man got the Indian allotment and the balance of the reserves mixed up in such a manner that he was afraid to touch any land. I have a letter written by the department to the Indian agent, instructing him how to proceed. It is dated Department of Indian Affairs, Jan. 21, 1908, and is signed by Frank Pedley:
Copy.
Department of Indian Affairs,
Ottawa, January 21, 1908.
Sir,-I beg to acknowledge the receipt of your communication of the 12th instant (No 2-37) in connection with the locations of Indians of the St. Peter reserve, in accordance with surrender, and given by them a short time ago, and in reply beg to say that action is being taken with as much expedition as possible to locate the Indians on the lands to which they may be found entitled, and you should notify them that there will be as little delay in arranging the matter as possible.
In connection with Indians disposing of or pledging their holdings, I beg to say that no transfer or pledge by any Indian will be in any way recognized by the department, and when it has been determined what land each Indian is entitled to receive, a jiatent for the same will be issued to such Indian, without regard to any claims by white men or others.
It is necessary to make this position of the department clear and as widely known as possible, as any] .recognition of rights by transfer would cause endless comj)lication, and in order to prevent same it is incumbent on the department to issue grants only to the Indians found entitled to receive same.
The representatives of the Indians and the department will deal with all claims to land in accordance with the provisions of the sur render.
Your obedient servant,

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
Deputy Superintendent General of Indian Adairs.
J. O. Lewis, Esq.
The point is this, that this letter was written to the Indian agent just at the time these lands were coming into the market-. A great many people around Selkirk wanted to purchase some of these lands, including a lot of my own friends, but as soon as it was made known that the department would not recognize any pledges or transfers given by the Indians until after the patents were issued, not one of these men would buy an acre of that land. Not one of these men bought an acre of this land. But very strange to say, the men who did purchase these lands, every one of them, were supporters of the hon. gentlemen opposite. Now these men must have received a tip from the department, or from somebody, that these pledges or transfers would be accepted. I ask the minister now if it is not a fact that every acre of this land was secured by the speculators before the patents were issued, in defiance of that letter written by Mr. Frank Pedley of the Indian Department? This is an absolute fact, Mr. Chairman, and this is one of the reasons why I ask the minister to open up this question and make a fair investigation. Now, if this letter had never been written and these lands had been thrown on the market, these frauds would not have taken place! Some of my friends were willing to pay $25 an acre for pieces of the land, but they knew that unless thev stood in with the Indian agent and the Indian Department, there was no guarantee they would ever receive their titles. I cannot understand how the minister, in face of the instructions given by his department, can get up and say that he assumes full responsibility for accepting the patents to-day, or accepting the transfers, and handing the patents over to those men who have purchased the lands in defiance of the instruction of the de-

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
partment. Why, according to this instruction not one of those allotments has been legally sold, and every one of them ought to be cancelled. Now so far as the Indian himself is concerned, it is the Indian I am fighting for to-day. I have no interest, nor have any of my friends, a dollar's interest in these lands, I am glad to say. I want to say this to the minister, that after this letter was written, one of the biggest speculators, one of the biggest holders' of this land to-day, came to Ottawa to interview somebody here, I do not know who. But I met him on the train going back, and he said to me: I have fixed the thing all right, I am going to buy the land, and if you like you can come in with me. I answered that it might be my duty, if I were elected, to criticise this matter in the House of Commons, and consequently I could not invest one dollar in the land. That fact, Mr. Chairman, is, I think, evidence that there was collusion between the purchasers and some official in the Department of Indian Affairs. These men who purchased those lands, who were putting up thousands and tens of thousands of dollars to be given to these Indians, do you not think- they knew that they were safe? There was no risk so far as they were concerned, they were going to get their patents in defiance of that letter, and they got them; and the only reason why the deal has not gone through is because the Land Titles Office at Winnipeg has held up every one of those patents on account of the alleged fraud on the f- ;e "f the whole transaction. I hold in my hand a petition from 110 Indians, some of those men that have been wronged, and I am going to present it to this House. I had no idea this discussion was coming on, and consequently I am not as well prepared for it as I would liked to have been, as there is other evidence that I will bring before the House later on. This letter was written from St. Peter's, November 1, 1909, and is addressed to myself:
We, the undersigned, beg to lay before you their following grievances. The surrender of the St. Peters reserve was made on- the 24th September, 1907. A few days after the surrender was made, land buyers came and bought land, first of all buying from the chief and council.
Then they hired the chief and council at $2 a day to remain in the offices, and around the offices, and to bring in other men who owned land and induce these Indians to sell to these men.
After this was done, then they were hired to influence their people to sell land, telling them until such time the issuing of patents, a proper bargain could be made, hence the land was sold, and the majority of Indians never made an application for their patents. However, the patents were issued, the In-Mr. BRADBURY
dians only heard of the same, never even having the privilege of seeing their patents.
Remember, Mr. Chairman, that this is an Indian letter, which fact explains the peculiarity of the language.
The Indians were entirely ignorant as to the nature of the documents they signed when selling land, for the reason that no proper interpretation was given at the time of sale or any other time, and that is the reason why there is so much complaint.	_
There is another matter which we think would be necessary to be understood properly. There were application forms at the Indian office, and each head of a family had to make an application in person for his or for her patent. This was never done, with hut a few exceptions. When issuing of patents there were another kind of forms at the Indian office \v li ieh had to he signed by the Indians before receiving their patents. This was never done, with but a few exceptions. We think it would be only proper to demand those forms in order that you may understand more fully as to the nature of the same.
The bon. gentleman says to-day it was 320 acres. These men are a little more moderate.
With regard to allotment of land, the chief received 196 acres. Each individual councillor received 136 acres, an ordinary Indian received 16 acres. Besides the chief and councillors received more money than the ordinary Indian.
Now, I want the minister to listen to this part:
The land buyers were the parties that selected the choice land, the Indians were simply onlookers. That is the treatment the Indians received from their so-called chief and councillors. In some instances the Indians were only receiving less than $2 per acre, some received $2.50, some $3, and some $4 and $5 to the acre, and some are entirely ignorant as to what sum they receited. We are all fully aware that our land was fully worth at least from $15 to $20 per acre.
Trusting that you will be able to understand the nature of our grievances, humbly requesting that you will use your influence to bring the matter before the House if possible, your petitioners will ever pray.
This is signed by 110 of the men that have been wronged. Now, Mr. Chairman, in face of all this evidence, in face of the many complaints that the minister himself has received personally, in face of the position that the chief justice takes, the man who negotiated this treaty, in face of the fact that the registrar at Winnipeg refused to allow these patents to go through is it not reasonable that I, the representative of that constituency, should ask the minister to grant an investigation to find out whether these statements are true, or false, to find out whether these Indians have been wronged or not. The minister cannot shield himself behind the fact that the Indian refused to allow him, or to allow﻿373

his officials, to insert in the surrender a clause which prevented the department from protecting them. These Indians were mere children, these Indians up to that time had been wards of the government. Every pound of tea they secured from the Indian Department was obtained through the Indian agent. Consequently, the Indian was utterly incompetent to deal with a matter of this kind, quite incompetent to dispose of an acre of land; but suddenly the department made him a landlord. I do not suppose that one of these Indians had ever owned an acre of land in his life before. The Indian had no idea of the value of what he possessed, but the chief and council were a little more intelligent and thoroughly unscrupulous. These men were purchased. In the first place, as the minister admits, they secured more lands than the others, 320 acres. The minister says the chief received this amount while the ordinary Indian, the man who had elected the chief and the council to protect his interests, received only sixteen acres of land. Why? I think it is a fair deduction to say that these Indians received that land in consideration of their inducing the rest of the band to agree to the surrender. In addition to that there is this other fact, which I wish to bring to the attention of the minister although he and his department are well aware of it: Although the term of office of the chief and council of these Indians expired in July in the very year of this transaction the department has refused to allow an election to take place in the band since. They have retained that chief and council there in defiance of the band. Petition after petition has been sent in asking that an election should be granted in order that they might have an opportunity of turning these men out of office. But in spite of all that the Indian Department keeps these men there. What for? To assist the land dealers in carrying out that nefarious transaction.	[DOT]
Does the hon. gentleman mean to say that the department here can keep a chief and council in office in defiance of the band?

That is what they have done. They have refused to allow the Indians in St. Peter's to have an election, although petition after petition has been sent in praying for justice. The band do not recognize the chief as their chief or the council as their councillors. Consequently they are practically in a disorganized condition to-day and the Department of Indian Affairs is directly responsible for it.
The whole transaction, from its very inception until the present time, has been notorious in Selkirk. Every one in Selkirk who knows anything about the manner in which the Indian agent and the lawyers employed by the Indian Department to protect these Indians have conducted this affair, realizes that a great wrong has been done to these people. I have here a statement brought down from the Department of Indian Affairs showing the fees paid to lawyers in this connection. One letter says:
I am directed to forward to you an account amounting to $1,509.65 received from the Hon. Chief Justice Howell, in connection with St. Peter's reserve.
There is another account of $1,093. Two of these lawyers, one being Mr. Heap, of Selkirk, were appointed to protect the interest of the Indians. Mr. Heap was looked on by the Indians as their solicitor and he advised them in many cases, but the strange part of the thing is that he was one of the land company who vTere purchasing this land. The whole transaction was carried on in a room not half the size of one of our committee rooms. The land buyers were in one end of the building, the Indian agent was in the other end, the lawyer was next door, and the chief and counsel were in attendance day after day bringing in these poor ignorant people and advising them to sell their land to this land company and these speculators. In face of the facts that have been adduced here today, in face of what the minister knows, I ask him again to grant a fair investigation into this transaction. It surely cannot do any harm to have an investigation into this transaction. It surely cannot do any harm to have an investigation. I feel satisfied in my own mind that wrong has been committed. I believe that these lands have passed into the hands of these purchasers at less than one-third, perhaps one-fourth of their value. I was surprised to hear the minister state that he believed that these lands had brought their full value at the sale. Let me illustrate for a moment. These lands were sold some time in November, 1908. The following spring the Indian reserve at Shoal Lake, hundreds of miles away, was put on the market. That land brought an average of $17.60 an acre, while the St. Peter's land, in the very garden of the province of Manitoba, has yielded the Indians muclt less than $5 an acre. After the lands were picked over, as I have stated in the earlier part of this discussion, the remnant of the reserve that was left to be sold by public competition, so-called-because it was only so-called, there was no competition about it-brought $5.68 an acre.
Let us take another illustration. At Beausejour, 35 miles east from Winnipeg, a school land sale was held the same season, and some of the same men who had secured these lands from the Indians paid $22 an acre for school lands by no means

equal to what they secured at St. Peter's for less than $5 from the Indian, and $5.68 at the so-called auction. In face of these facts it must be apparent to the hon. gentleman that the Indians have not received a fair price for their lands. The question arises, what is the responsibility of the department? The hon. minister says they have no responsibility. They made a deal with the Indian to surrender bis land. He agreed to take the 16 acres and another reserve, and as far as that allotment was concerned, he could do as he pleased, the department had no authority, no control and consequently did not intend to interfere. 1 think that is a short-sighted position. The Indian is a ward of the government and if he becomes pauperized this country must come to his assistance and feed him; consequently it is the duty of the department to see that he gets a fair value for every acre of his land. In addition to all these things the hon. minister knows, I am satisfied there are documents in his department which will show beyond ariv doubt, that there are to-day even more serious complaints from the Indians than those I have made regarding this transaction. This petition I received only yesterday and I am informed by letter that the chief himself, the man who was an instrument in the hands of these land sharks has since declared that he helped to deceive the band, that he did not tell the band the truth, that when these lands were being purchased the explanation given to the Indian in nearly every case was that the Indian was not signing away his lands but only signing an agreement that when the patents were issued, he would give the man advancing him the money, the first chance to buy the lands at the price fixed by the Indian.
Now, Mr. Chairman, in face of these facts, because I believe they are facts, I cannot see how the minister can hesitate one moment to grant a fair in-, vestigation. I do not think there is any doubt at all that it can be proven beyond any question that the Indian has been deceived. I do not think there is any doubt that when he signed these agreements he did not realize that he was signing away his rights to his land. He thought that these speculators were giving him an advance, loaning him money on his land. Do not overlook the point that the Indian was misled by the department itself. The department told the Indian that until such time as the patents could be issued the Indian had nothing to sell. The department is on record advising the Indians that they had nothing to sell until their patents^ were issued. Consequently the Indian did not realize that he was selling his land or that he was disposing of his rights. He said to himself: Here is the letter; the Mr. BRADBURY.
Indian agent tells me I have nothing to sell, and I am only signing an agreement that when I get something to sell I will make a bargain with these men who want my land. There is no question at all that that is the position that the Indian took in the matter. That is what he thought, and when you realize that every one of these agreements is an absolute transfer secured in defiance of this letter you will acknowledge that the minister has the authority and the right to step in and cancel every one of these agreements and you will acknowledge that it is his duty to do so. I have taken up a good deal more of the time of the committee than I expected to do. There is a good deal more to be said on this question, and unless the minister is prepared to grant a fair investigation I can only promise him that this debate cannot end here, because there are matters of very great importance that will have to be ventilated, and it would take up a good deal more of the time of the House than we have taken up this afternoon. But it is only fair, I think, if the minister were inclined to be fair, and he usually is, to ask that he will undertake to have this question thoroughly inquired into. I cannot understand why the minister, in a case, of this kind, is hesitating. There must be something behind it that we cannot see, for if there ever was a case for interference by the trustees of these people it is this one. I feel satisfied that the minister ought to step in and tell us to-night that he will give a fair and impartial investigation into all these facts and see that the Indian gets a fair price for his land.
Some resolutions reported.

speechtext: It has been intimated that very many of the members on both sides of the House have engagements which will prevent their being present to-night, and as we are likely to have a thin House I beg to move that the House do now adjourn.
